new.title: Graze through fourteen kitchens at Foodhall Breda
new.desc: A few steps from the harbour, Foodhall Breda gathers 14 small kitchens and a central bar under one roof. Everyone orders from a different counter and you all eat at the same shared tables, which makes it the easiest place in town for a group that cannot agree.
new.tip: It is closed on Mondays and opens at noon the rest of the week. Come early on Friday or Saturday evening, when the tables fill quickly.

new.title: Eat a cone of fresh fries at Cafetaria De Toren
new.desc: In the lane that runs up to the tower of the Grote Kerk, Cafetaria De Toren cuts and fries its potatoes fresh instead of using frozen chips. It is a proper Dutch snack bar, with a long list of sauces and fried snacks to go with the fries.
new.tip: Order a friet speciaal, with mayonnaise, curry ketchup and raw onion, and eat it on the Kerkplein around the corner.

new.title: Have a drink by the village pump on the Ginnekenmarkt
new.desc: Ginneken was a separate village until Breda annexed it in 1942, and locals still call it 't Ginneke. Its little market square is ringed with café terraces around the old village pump, with the Sint-Laurentiuskerk of 1902 by Joseph Cuypers and Jan Stuyt rising behind.
new.tip: Cycle here along the Ginnekenweg from the centre in about ten minutes. Around 1900 this was a holiday village full of hotels, which explains the grand houses on the way.

new.title: Step inside the neoclassical Sint-Antoniuskathedraal
new.desc: Breda's Catholic cathedral looks nothing like a Dutch church: Pieter Huijsers designed it in 1837 with a facade of Doric, Ionic and Corinthian columns stacked above each other. It served as cathedral from 1853 to 1876 and took the title back in 2001. Inside, twelve columns stand for the twelve apostles.
new.tip: Look for the carved wooden pulpit showing the life of Saint Anthony of Padua. The church stands in the Sint Janstraat, two minutes from the Grote Markt.

new.title: Picnic in the old castle garden of Park Valkenberg
new.desc: The park between the station and the old town was once the garden of Breda Castle. Today it has a pond with a big fountain, remains of the towers of the medieval town wall and the Baroniemonument of 1905 by Pierre Cuypers at the Willemstraat entrance.
new.tip: In the north of the park stands 't T Huis by artist John Körmeling, a glass pavilion whose facade lists soup, fries, ice cream and cake, most of which it does not sell. A side gate leads straight into the Begijnhof.

new.title: Thank the Polish liberators at the Maczek Memorial
new.desc: Breda was liberated in 1944 by the 1st Polish Armoured Division of General Stanisław Maczek, and the city has never forgotten it. This memorial museum opened in 2020 behind the Polish military cemetery and shows Maczek's own uniform, donated by his children, alongside original wartime objects.
new.tip: It only opens on a few afternoons a week, so check the days before you go. Walk through the cemetery next door first.

new.title: Follow the brass bands at the Breda Jazz Festival
new.desc: Since 1971 the old town has turned into one big jazz club for four days, starting on Ascension Day. Around 250,000 people come for traditional jazz, blues, zydeco and swing on outdoor stages at the Havermarkt, the Kerkplein, the Grote Markt and a pontoon by the Spanjaardsgat, and the street concerts are free.
new.tip: Ascension Day moves with Easter, so the festival falls in May or early June. The stage at 't Sas by the harbour is a good place to start.

new.title: Walk into the Markdal from the Duivelsbrug
new.desc: At the Duivelsbrug in Ginneken the city stops and the valley of the river Mark begins, running south to the Belgian border. The river was straightened in the 1960s and has been given its bends back since the 1990s, which brought back kingfishers, sand martins and storks, and beavers since 2019.
new.tip: The first bridge here dates from 1611. Look for the poem stones along the river, resting places meant to make you stop and look.

new.title: Work through the beer list at Biercafé Kandinsky
new.desc: Kandinsky is the beer lovers' pub of Tilburg, with a list of around 200 beers, many of them on tap and each served in its own glass. The walls are covered with enamel beer signs and the music stays low enough to talk.
new.tip: It opens in the afternoon, at three on weekdays and at two at the weekend. Ask the bar staff what is new on tap rather than reading the whole list.

new.title: Have dinner in a train carriage at Eetbar De Wagon
new.desc: In the Spoorzone, the former workshops of the Dutch railways behind Tilburg station, two train carriages from the last century have been turned into a restaurant. The kitchen serves familiar, generous dishes for lunch and dinner.
new.tip: It opens at noon. Combine it with the LocHal and the other old railway halls, which are a short walk away.
new.q: Eetbar de Wagon, Burgemeester Brokxlaan, Tilburg

new.title: Find the Heikese kerk on the Oude Markt
new.desc: The Sint-Dionysiuskerk is the mother church of Tilburg, on the spot where the parish has stood since the Middle Ages: in 1232 the Duke of Brabant gave its rights to Tongerlo Abbey. The present building dates from 1838, and everybody calls it the Heikese kerk after the old hamlet of 't Heike.
new.tip: Walk around to compare the plain nave with the later Neo-Gothic west front. The Paleis-Raadhuis is a few steps away.

new.title: Spend a sunny afternoon in the Spoorpark
new.desc: Tilburg's newest park was finished in 2019 on an abandoned shunting yard, after residents came up with the plan themselves. Its almost ten hectares hold a lookout tower, a stream, sports fields, a café and even a city campsite, and some of the old rails still run through the grass.
new.tip: The park is open daily from eight in the morning until ten at night, and an hour longer in summer. The main entrance is on the east side at the Sint-Ceciliastraat.

new.title: Watch a house drive around the Hasselt roundabout
new.desc: In the middle of the Hasseltrotonde a full-size house, ten metres high, slowly circles the roundabout on rails and takes almost an hour for one lap. Artist John Körmeling's Draaiend Huis has been turning since 2008, and squatters briefly moved in a year later in protest at its cost.
new.tip: It moves so slowly that you only notice when you look away and back. Take a photo, wait ten minutes and take another.

new.title: Cross the Brabant Sahara of the Loonse en Drunense Duinen
new.desc: North of Tilburg lies a drift sand landscape that is exceptionally large for Northern Europe: bare dunes up to 24 metres high, ringed by pine forest. The sand started to blow in the late Middle Ages after the heath was overgrazed, and it buried the village of Westloon. Today it is the heart of the Van Gogh National Park.
new.tip: Start at Bosch en Duin in Udenhout, where a paved path of one kilometre leads to a viewpoint over the sand. Bring water on sunny days, as there is no shade out there.

new.title: Go on safari at Beekse Bergen
new.desc: Between Tilburg and Hilvarenbeek lies the largest wildlife park of the Benelux by area, with about a hundred species. Zebras, giraffes and ostriches share wide open plains, and there are lions, rhinos, elephants and cheetahs as well.
new.tip: You can cross the park on foot, in your own car, by safari bus or by boat. Do the walking route early in the day and save the drive for when your legs are tired.

new.title: Learn to live with water at the Biesbosch MuseumEiland
new.desc: This museum sits on its own island in the middle of the Biesbosch National Park, the freshwater tidal delta that formed after the Sint-Elisabeth flood of 1421. It tells how people lived from reed, willow and fish here, and how line-crossers smuggled people through the creeks in the Second World War.
new.tip: Combine the museum with the whisper boat, a quiet electric trip of 75 minutes into the creeks. In the winter months the museum is closed on Mondays.

new.title: Stand under the Gevangenpoort in Bergen op Zoom
new.desc: The Gevangenpoort, built around 1335, is the oldest monument in Bergen op Zoom and the only town gate that survives. Its two stout towers still have the slits made for crossbows. When the harbour quarter was walled in 1484 the gate ended up inside the town and lost its job.
new.tip: See both faces: the town side on the Lievevrouwestraat and the rounder, grimmer side towards the Westersingel.

new.title: Look up at the Peperbus on the Grote Markt of Bergen op Zoom
new.desc: The tower of the Sint-Gertrudiskerk is nicknamed the Peperbus, the pepper pot, after the cap it got in the 18th century. The base dates from about 1370. A French bombardment wrecked the church in 1747 and a fire gutted it again in 1972, and each time the town rebuilt it.
new.tip: Inside, notice the flat steel roof over the nave that replaced the burnt wooden vaults. The terraces on the Grote Markt give the best view of the tower.
new.q: Sint-Gertrudiskerk, Grote Markt, Bergen op Zoom

new.title: Lunch among the convent vines at Wijnhuis De Blauwe Camer
new.desc: The Norbertine sisters of Sint-Catharinadal have lived in the slotje De Blauwe Camer outside Oosterhout since 1647, and they have planted a vineyard on their land. In a farmhouse on the grounds, this restaurant serves seasonal lunches and set menus between the vines, using the sisters' vegetable and herb garden.
new.tip: It is open from Wednesday to Sunday, from noon. Ask for a glass of the convent's own wine and stop at the convent shop before you leave.
